The problem

Dental imaging is information-rich. The workflow around it isn't.

A single visit can produce a panoramic scan, a set of bitewings, and two years of prior studies to check against. None of that is a shortage of information — it's a shortage of time to look at all of it, tooth by tooth, film by film.

  1. 01Open the patient record and locate the relevant image
  2. 02Step through each tooth individually, front to back
  3. 03Flag anything that looks worth a second look
  4. 04Pull up prior studies and compare by eye
  5. 05Write it up, then explain it to the patient in plain terms
Oralytix doesn't remove a step from that list — it does step 2 through 4 first, so the dentist's time goes to judgment, not scanning.
How a scan moves through the system

Nine steps, from upload to chart note

This is the actual path an image takes — not a metaphor. Each stage either checks the image or hands a decision back to the dentist.

01

Image received

Bitewing, periapical, panoramic, or CBCT — pulled in from the sensor or uploaded directly.

02

Quality check

Exposure, positioning, and cropping are checked before analysis runs, so a blurry film doesn't produce a false-confident finding.

03

Tooth detection

Individual teeth are identified and numbered, giving every later finding a fixed address in the mouth.

04

AI analysis

The model looks for candidate findings — caries, existing restorations, periapical changes — across the full image.

05

Visual highlighting

Candidate regions are outlined directly on the image, not described in a separate report.

06

Historical comparison

Prior studies for the same patient are aligned automatically, and regions that changed are marked.

07

Dentist review

Every finding sits in a queue of three actions: confirm, dismiss, or modify. Nothing is written to the chart unreviewed.

08

Clinical documentation

Confirmed findings are turned into structured notes in the dentist's own phrasing, ready to edit.

09

Imaging history updates

The patient's timeline updates automatically, so the next visit starts with full context already in place.

AI assists. Dentist decides.
Oralytix never writes a diagnosis to the chart. It surfaces candidates; the dentist accepts, edits, or dismisses each one.

Feature spotlight

Findings live on the image, not in a separate report

Instead of a text line reading "possible caries, lower right," the region itself is outlined on the radiograph. Click it, and a panel opens with the tooth number, the finding, and the model's confidence — the same interaction shown in the scan above.

  • Click-through, not scroll-through
    The dentist inspects flagged regions directly instead of scanning the whole image from scratch.
  • Confidence shown plainly
    Every finding carries a model-confidence figure, so low-certainty candidates read differently than high-certainty ones.
  • Explainable by design
    Because findings are anchored to a visible region, they're easy to check against the image, not just take on faith.

Patient communication

The same finding, explained twice

A radiograph is easy for a dentist to read and hard for almost everyone else. Patient mode keeps the technical view for the chart, and swaps in plain language for the conversation across the room — the dentist chooses what the patient sees.

Clinical view

Radiolucency, distal surface, tooth 46. Consistent with early-stage carious lesion. Recommend restorative evaluation.

The rule the product is built around

AI assists. The dentist decides.

Oralytix doesn't diagnose, and it doesn't get the last word. It's built to make the dentist's read faster and less easy to miss something in — never to replace the read itself.

  • Every AI finding is labeled as a candidate for review, never a diagnosis.
  • Nothing is written to the patient chart until a dentist confirms, edits, or dismisses it.
  • Model confidence is always visible next to the finding, not hidden behind a plain "detected" label.
Why now

The timing isn't incidental

  • 1

    Caries detection is validated research, not a bet

    AI-assisted caries and abnormality detection is one of the more thoroughly studied problems in dental imaging — the science exists to build on, not invent from scratch.

  • 2

    GPU inference is cheap enough to run per-scan

    Serving a model per radiograph, at seconds-not-minutes latency, is now a reasonable cost — it wasn't five years ago.

  • 3

    Practices are already digitizing imaging

    Digital sensors and PACS-style storage are now the norm in most practices, not the exception — the raw material an AI review needs already exists in the workflow.

  • 4

    Imaging AI is entering clinical use, with a regulatory path

    Cleared dental AI systems already return visual findings like bounding boxes and segmentation outlines — the regulatory category exists and is being actively used, not theoretical.

The roadmap

Built to earn the next capability, not launch with it

Each phase only starts once the one before it has been trusted in real practices. Nothing here is a feature list — it's the order things have to happen in.

Phase 01 Now

Prove the read

The first release stays narrow on purpose: caries and abnormality candidates, one of the more thoroughly studied problems in dental imaging AI. Every finding routes through confirm, dismiss, or modify before it touches a chart. This phase is about earning trust one scan at a time — not covering every condition on day one.

Quality assistant Tooth detection Candidate detection Overlay review
Phase 02 Next

Prove the pattern

Once the first-pass read is trusted, historical comparison stops being two images side by side and becomes automatic change detection — flagging what's actually different, not just what's there. Structured summaries start drafting themselves from confirmed findings, and model performance gets benchmarked across practices, not just within one.

Automatic change detection Structured summaries Cross-practice benchmarking
Phase 03 Later

Prove the system

With a validated read and a validated pattern, the model earns a harder job: flagging which patients are due a closer look before their next visit, not just reading the scan already in front of it. Support extends to CBCT and deeper integration with the practice's existing management software, so the review lives where the rest of the chart already does.

Predictive follow-up CBCT support Practice-system integration
Why this needs real infrastructure

Sized for medical images and inference load, not a demo

Analyzing full-resolution radiographs at practice volume, with a latency budget measured in seconds, is a cloud-compute and GPU problem before it's anything else.

AWS

Cloud infrastructure

Storage, compute, and monitoring for every scan
Amazon S3 Stores encrypted radiographs, intraoral photos, and the annotated reference datasets used to validate each model release.
Amazon ECS Runs the AI inference services that analyze every uploaded scan, scaled independently from the rest of the application.
Amazon RDS Stores patient-independent operational metadata: tooth-numbering schemas, model version history, and the audit trail behind every confirm, dismiss, or modify action.
AWS Lambda Handles event-driven processing — triggering quality checks and comparison jobs the moment a new image lands in storage.
Amazon CloudWatch Monitors inference latency and system health, so a slow model shows up before it reaches chairside review.
Amazon Bedrock (planned) Planned for Phase 2 — generating the structured summary drafts described in the roadmap, once historical comparison is validated.
NVIDIA

GPU compute

Training and serving the imaging models
CUDA Powers GPU-accelerated training of the caries and abnormality detection models on annotated radiograph datasets.
TensorRT Optimizes inference latency — the difference between a first-pass review that takes seconds and one that takes minutes.
Triton Inference Server Serves the tooth-detection, quality-check, and candidate-finding models concurrently, without standing up separate infrastructure for each.
NVIDIA GPUs Accelerate image analysis across panoramic, bitewing, and periapical inputs at the volume a multi-chair practice actually produces.
NVIDIA Jetson (roadmap) On the roadmap for Phase 3 — edge inference for practices with limited connectivity, as CBCT support expands the volume of data per study.

The imaging review bottleneck described earlier isn't specific to one practice — it exists everywhere dental radiographs get read.

Source: industry market research estimates, 2025

Solo and small practices

The majority of U.S. dental practices are still solo or small-group — practice ownership has declined from 85% to 73% since 2005, but most reads still happen without a second set of eyes. This is where a first-pass review changes the workflow the most.

DSOs and group practices

Dental support organizations now account for a fast-growing share of U.S. practices and lean on standardized workflows across many locations. Consistent, structured findings are what makes an AI review scale across a chain instead of one office.

Target users

  • General and pediatric dental practices
  • Dental support organizations (DSOs)
  • Practice management software partners

Revenue model

  • Per-seat monthly subscription, priced by chair count
  • Usage-based pricing for high-volume DSO imaging centers
  • Integration fees for practice-management-software partners

Growth plan

  • Start with a small cohort of solo and small-group practices
  • Expand within a single DSO network once the workflow is validated
  • Then expand by region, following where imaging is already digitized

A note on how this is classified

For practices evaluating the product

Software that analyzes radiological images falls within a medical-device category in the United States, and a number of AI-assisted dental imaging tools — including ones that return visual findings like bounding boxes or segmentation outlines — are already in clinical use under that framework.

Oralytix is built around that reality rather than around it: findings are presented as candidates for review, not as diagnoses, and every one requires a dentist's decision before it becomes part of the record.
